analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set all pollution standards strong enough to protect children's health.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without ever getting a hearing, a vote, or a single further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten how the EPA assesses pollution risks, requiring the agency to evaluate threats to children, pregnant women, the elderly, and the chronically ill separately from risks to healthy adults. It would have required every EPA standard to protect vulnerable groups with an added margin of safety, forced a review of at least 20 existing standards for revision, and created public right-to-know lists of substances found where children go and of safer alternatives. Products not on the safer list would have been banned from federal buildings and lands.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, pregnant women, the elderly, and people with serious illnesses, whose greater sensitivity to pesticides and toxic pollutants would have had to be accounted for in every EPA risk assessment and standard. Families would also have gained access to plain-language information about toxic substances in homes, schools, day care centers, and parks.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to evaluate risks to children and other vulnerable groups in every risk assessment and standard, and to ensure standards protect them with an adequate margin of safety [S2] [S3].

Cites a National Academy of Sciences finding that existing risk assessment methods typically do not consider risks to children, so current pesticide tolerances often fail to adequately protect infants and children [S3].

Directs EPA to publish a peer-reviewed list of substances found in homes, schools, day care centers, malls, theaters, and parks that pose known, likely, or suspected risks to children, plus a list of safer-for-children alternatives, a family right-to-know kit, and exposure-reduction guidelines, all posted publicly and on the Internet [S2] [S3].

Requires EPA to reevaluate and propose at least 20 existing public health and environmental standards for revision, completing revisions within 15 years, and to ban products excluded from the safer-for-children list from all federally owned or controlled properties [S2] [S3].
Coordinates federal research on the health effects and toxicity of pesticides, including inert ingredients, and other pollutants on children and vulnerable groups [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide and chemical manufacturers, whose products could have landed on the risky-substances list, faced stricter child-specific testing and risk assessments, and been barred from federal properties. Federal agencies and taxpayers would have borne the cost of switching to safer products and funding the research and public-information programs.

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates sweeping new assessment, listing, reporting, and standard-revision duties for EPA and partner agencies with an open-ended appropriation of 'such sums as are necessary,' a real cost to taxpayers and a significant regulatory workload [S3].

Requiring a separate child-focused assessment for every EPA decision and an added safety margin in all standards could restrict the use of products that are safe for most adults, raising costs for agriculture and public agencies; the bill itself acknowledges that key child-specific exposure and bioaccumulation data do not yet exist, so some standards might have been revised ahead of the science [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside for children, who face measurably higher risks from the same exposures, was large and the mechanism reasonable: it did not ban products outright but required EPA to look at children's risks explicitly and publish information families could use. The main costs were regulatory workload and compliance costs for chemical and pesticide makers, plus the federal procurement shift. An honest supporter would concede that the deadline-driven revision of 20 standards outpaced the available child-specific data, which is why the bill paired the mandate with new research funding.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 1997 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer, joined by Senator Frank Lautenberg, introduced the Children's Environmental Protection Act on April 16, 1997 [S1] [S3].
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction [S5].
The full action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide and chemical manufacturers were better off, since they avoided child-specific risk assessments, a published list of products posing risks to children, and a ban on their excluded products from federal properties. Children and families gained nothing, because the protections never advanced beyond a committee referral.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Children's Environmental Protection Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; original co-sponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined Boxer in introducing the bill.

against.name: Sen. John Chafee
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die there.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor, the original co-sponsor, and all four cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill; no roll-call was ever held, so the partisan split was never formally tested.

industries.note: The bill targets pesticides directly: child-specific risk assessments, a published list of pesticides posing risks to children, a peer-reviewed safer-alternatives list, and a ban on excluded products from federal properties. Stricter standards could have pulled products off the market and increased testing costs.

Hazardous substances under CERCLA would have faced mandatory evaluation of risks to children and vulnerable groups with an added safety margin, plus public right-to-know lists naming products found in places children go.

New research mandates on pesticide toxicity, including inert ingredients, could have led to tighter tolerances affecting farm chemical use, but the bill imposed no direct restrictions on agricultural use itself.
